case_info.scenario: A 9-year-old girl presented with a 4-year history of asymptomatic, irregular pigmented lesions on the vulva and was initially diagnosed with a nevus at a local clinic. Physical examination revealed clustered, irregular, 6-mm dark blue papules with a smooth surface, located on the inferomedial aspect of the left labia minora (Figure 1A). The patient reported no pruritus, pain, abnormal discharge, or prior local trauma. Her personal and family history was unremarkable. No tenderness was elicited on palpation, and there was no inguinal lymphadenopathy or involvement of other mucosal sites. An excisional biopsy was performed for histopathological evaluation (Figure 1B).
case_info.caption: A, Clustered, irregular, 6-mm dark blue papules with a smooth surface on the left labia minora. B, Histopathologic examination reveals increased numbers of glands and tubular structures of varying calibers within the dermis, arranged in a disorganized organoid pattern and lined by a single layer of cuboidal to columnar eosinophilic cells exhibiting apocrine-type decapitation secretion (hematoxylin-eosin staining, original magnification ×100).
case_info.explanation: Histopathological examination revealed epidermal hyperplasia with mild spongiosis. The underlying dermis contained increased numbers of glands and tubular structures of varying calibers, arranged in a somewhat disorganized organoid architecture. These structures were lined by a single layer of cuboidal to columnar eosinophilic cells exhibiting apocrine-type decapitation secretion (Figure 1B). A peripheral layer of attenuated myoepithelial cells was readily identified. Prominent granular melanin deposits were observed along the luminal surfaces of the glands and within the adjacent stroma, which were positive for Fontana-Masson stain. Immunohistochemical analysis confirmed epithelial cell immunoreactivity for both pan-cytokeratin and cytokeratin 7. SOX-10 staining, which highlights nuclei of melanocytes and myoepithelial cells, provided a clear distinction between these and the nuclei of the apocrine epithelium (Figure 2). Furthermore, Melan-A staining highlighted dendritic melanocytes distributed within the glandular cuboidal epithelium and scattered throughout the reticular dermis. The overall morphological and immunophenotypic features supported a diagnosis of pigmented apocrine hamartoma (PAH). The lesion was completely excised, and the patient remains asymptomatic under regular postoperative monitoring. Apocrine hamartoma, also known as apocrine nevus, is a rare benign skin disorder characterized by the abnormal growth of mature, dilated apocrine glands that extend from the reticular dermis into the subcutaneous tissue. While it can occur as an isolated lesion, it is more often seen as part of nevus sebaceus. Clinically, these lesions appear as single or multiple papules or nodules, mainly in the axillary region, followed by the chest, temple, and neck.1When pigmented lesions with similar features appear in the vulvar area, this condition is specifically called PAH, representing a distinct histopathologic variant marked by disorganized growth of melanin-containing apocrine glands and ducts arranged in an organoid pattern. The melanin pigmentation seems to result from dendritic melanocytes colonizing the apocrine glands. These melanocytes can be seen on standard hematoxylin and eosin staining but are much clearer with immunohistochemical and special stains.2Melanin shows positive staining with Fontana-Masson and negative staining with Prussian blue, differentiating it from hemosiderin deposits. The current case was found on the vulva, initially raising concern for melanoma because of its pronounced pigmentation. To date and to our knowledge, fewer than 10 cases of PAH have been documented in the literature, all in female patients aged 8 to 21 years.2-6Surgical excision represents the treatment of choice for PAH, and to date, no recurrences have been reported following complete resection. This favorable outcome underscores the importance of definitive surgical management for both diagnosis and treatment. The clinical presentation of pigmented vulvar lesions involving melanocytes—whether dendritic or not—is associated with a broad spectrum of conditions. These range from benign entities such as melanocytic nevi and vulvar melanosis to malignant neoplasms, including melanoma and pigmented basal cell carcinoma. The absence of a proliferation of melanocytic nests or atypical melanocytes rules out a melanocytic nevus and melanoma, respectively. The possibility of pigmented basal cell carcinoma was excluded due to the lack of characteristic basaloid islands with peripheral palisading, retraction artifacts, and stromal mucin deposition. In the present case, the pigment was confined to the apocrine epithelium and luminal debris, rather than within basaloid tumor islands. Furthermore, the lesion’s architectural features differed from those of hidradenoma papilliferum. Although both entities originate from apocrine glands, hidradenoma papilliferum is characterized by well-circumscribed, cystic spaces with intricate papillary projections and a fibrous stroma, features absent in this case.7 In summary, PAH is a clinically important condition because it can resemble malignant pigmented vulvar lesions. Although rare, it should be considered in the differential diagnosis of pigmented vulvar lesions in young women and girls. Accurate diagnosis relies on clinical suspicion, detailed histopathological examination, and the careful application of immunohistochemical tests to prevent misdiagnosis and inform appropriate treatment.

The underlying dermis contained increased numbers of glands and tubular structures of varying calibers, arranged in a somewhat disorganized organoid architecture. These structures were lined by a single layer of cuboidal to columnar eosinophilic cells exhibiting apocrine-type decapitation secretion (Figure 1B). A peripheral layer of attenuated myoepithelial cells was readily identified. Prominent granular melanin deposits were observed along the luminal surfaces of the glands and within the adjacent stroma, which were positive for Fontana-Masson stain. Immunohistochemical analysis confirmed epithelial cell immunoreactivity for both pan-cytokeratin and cytokeratin 7. SOX-10 staining, which highlights nuclei of melanocytes and myoepithelial cells, provided a clear distinction between these and the nuclei of the apocrine epithelium (Figure 2). Furthermore, Melan-A staining highlighted dendritic melanocytes distributed within the glandular cuboidal epithelium and scattered throughout the reticular dermis. The overall morphological and immunophenotypic features supported a diagnosis of pigmented apocrine hamartoma (PAH). The lesion was completely excised, and the patient remains asymptomatic under regular postoperative monitoring. Apocrine hamartoma, also known as apocrine nevus, is a rare benign skin disorder characterized by the abnormal growth of mature, dilated apocrine glands that extend from the reticular dermis into the subcutaneous tissue. While it can occur as an isolated lesion, it is more often seen as part of nevus sebaceus. Clinically, these lesions appear as single or multiple papules or nodules, mainly in the axillary region, followed by the chest, temple, and neck.1When pigmented lesions with similar features appear in the vulvar area, this condition is specifically called PAH, representing a distinct histopathologic variant marked by disorganized growth of melanin-containing apocrine glands and ducts arranged in an organoid pattern. The melanin pigmentation seems to result from dendritic melanocytes colonizing the apocrine glands. These melanocytes can be seen on standard hematoxylin and eosin staining but are much clearer with immunohistochemical and special stains.2Melanin shows positive staining with Fontana-Masson and negative staining with Prussian blue, differentiating it from hemosiderin deposits. The current case was found on the vulva, initially raising concern for melanoma because of its pronounced pigmentation. To date and to our knowledge, fewer than 10 cases of PAH have been documented in the literature, all in female patients aged 8 to 21 years.2-6Surgical excision represents the treatment of choice for PAH, and to date, no recurrences have been reported following complete resection. This favorable outcome underscores the importance of definitive surgical management for both diagnosis and treatment. The clinical presentation of pigmented vulvar lesions involving melanocytes—whether dendritic or not—is associated with a broad spectrum of conditions. These range from benign entities such as melanocytic nevi and vulvar melanosis to malignant neoplasms, including melanoma and pigmented basal cell carcinoma. The absence of a proliferation of melanocytic nests or atypical melanocytes rules out a melanocytic nevus and melanoma, respectively. The possibility of pigmented basal cell carcinoma was excluded due to the lack of characteristic basaloid islands with peripheral palisading, retraction artifacts, and stromal mucin deposition. In the present case, the pigment was confined to the apocrine epithelium and luminal debris, rather than within basaloid tumor islands. Furthermore, the lesion’s architectural features differed from those of hidradenoma papilliferum. Although both entities originate from apocrine glands, hidradenoma papilliferum is characterized by well-circumscribed, cystic spaces with intricate papillary projections and a fibrous stroma, features absent in this case.7 In summary, PAH is a clinically important condition because it can resemble malignant pigmented vulvar lesions. The underlying dermis contained increased numbers of glands and tubular structures of varying calibers, arranged in a somewhat disorganized organoid architecture. These structures were lined by a single layer of cuboidal to columnar eosinophilic cells exhibiting apocrine-type decapitation secretion (Figure 1B). A peripheral layer of attenuated myoepithelial cells was readily identified. Prominent granular melanin deposits were observed along the luminal surfaces of the glands and within the adjacent stroma, which were positive for Fontana-Masson stain. Immunohistochemical analysis confirmed epithelial cell immunoreactivity for both pan-cytokeratin and cytokeratin 7. SOX-10 staining, which highlights nuclei of melanocytes and myoepithelial cells, provided a clear distinction between these and the nuclei of the apocrine epithelium (Figure 2). Furthermore, Melan-A staining highlighted dendritic melanocytes distributed within the glandular cuboidal epithelium and scattered throughout the reticular dermis. The overall morphological and immunophenotypic features supported a diagnosis of pigmented apocrine hamartoma (PAH). The lesion was completely excised, and the patient remains asymptomatic under regular postoperative monitoring. Apocrine hamartoma, also known as apocrine nevus, is a rare benign skin disorder characterized by the abnormal growth of mature, dilated apocrine glands that extend from the reticular dermis into the subcutaneous tissue. While it can occur as an isolated lesion, it is more often seen as part of nevus sebaceus. Clinically, these lesions appear as single or multiple papules or nodules, mainly in the axillary region, followed by the chest, temple, and neck.1When pigmented lesions with similar features appear in the vulvar area, this condition is specifically called PAH, representing a distinct histopathologic variant marked by disorganized growth of melanin-containing apocrine glands and ducts arranged in an organoid pattern. The melanin pigmentation seems to result from dendritic melanocytes colonizing the apocrine glands. These melanocytes can be seen on standard hematoxylin and eosin staining but are much clearer with immunohistochemical and special stains.2Melanin shows positive staining with Fontana-Masson and negative staining with Prussian blue, differentiating it from hemosiderin deposits. The current case was found on the vulva, initially raising concern for melanoma because of its pronounced pigmentation. To date and to our knowledge, fewer than 10 cases of PAH have been documented in the literature, all in female patients aged 8 to 21 years.2-6Surgical excision represents the treatment of choice for PAH, and to date, no recurrences have been reported following complete resection. The clinical presentation of pigmented vulvar lesions involving melanocytes—whether dendritic or not—is associated with a broad spectrum of conditions. These range from benign entities such as melanocytic nevi and vulvar melanosis to malignant neoplasms, including melanoma and pigmented basal cell carcinoma. The absence of a proliferation of melanocytic nests or atypical melanocytes rules out a melanocytic nevus and melanoma, respectively. The possibility of pigmented basal cell carcinoma was excluded due to the lack of characteristic basaloid islands with peripheral palisading, retraction artifacts, and stromal mucin deposition. In the present case, the pigment was confined to the apocrine epithelium and luminal debris, rather than within basaloid tumor islands. case_info.explanation: Histopathological examination revealed epidermal hyperplasia with mild spongiosis. The underlying dermis contained increased numbers of glands and tubular structures of varying calibers, arranged in a somewhat disorganized organoid architecture. These structures were lined by a single layer of cuboidal to columnar eosinophilic cells exhibiting apocrine-type decapitation secretion (Figure 1B). A peripheral layer of attenuated myoepithelial cells was readily identified. Prominent granular melanin deposits were observed along the luminal surfaces of the glands and within the adjacent stroma, which were positive for Fontana-Masson stain. Immunohistochemical analysis confirmed epithelial cell immunoreactivity for both pan-cytokeratin and cytokeratin 7. SOX-10 staining, which highlights nuclei of melanocytes and myoepithelial cells, provided a clear distinction between these and the nuclei of the apocrine epithelium (Figure 2). Furthermore, Melan-A staining highlighted dendritic melanocytes distributed within the glandular cuboidal epithelium and scattered throughout the reticular dermis. The overall morphological and immunophenotypic features supported a diagnosis of pigmented apocrine hamartoma (PAH). The lesion was completely excised, and the patient remains asymptomatic under regular postoperative monitoring. Apocrine hamartoma, also known as apocrine nevus, is a rare benign skin disorder characterized by the abnormal growth of mature, dilated apocrine glands that extend from the reticular dermis into the subcutaneous tissue. While it can occur as an isolated lesion, it is more often seen as part of nevus sebaceus. Clinically, these lesions appear as single or multiple papules or nodules, mainly in the axillary region, followed by the chest, temple, and neck.1When pigmented lesions with similar features appear in the vulvar area, this condition is specifically called PAH, representing a distinct histopathologic variant marked by disorganized growth of melanin-containing apocrine glands and ducts arranged in an organoid pattern. The melanin pigmentation seems to result from dendritic melanocytes colonizing the apocrine glands. These melanocytes can be seen on standard hematoxylin and eosin staining but are much clearer with immunohistochemical and special stains.2Melanin shows positive staining with Fontana-Masson and negative staining with Prussian blue, differentiating it from hemosiderin deposits. The current case was found on the vulva, initially raising concern for melanoma because of its pronounced pigmentation. To date and to our knowledge, fewer than 10 cases of PAH have been documented in the literature, all in female patients aged 8 to 21 years.2-6Surgical excision represents the treatment of choice for PAH, and to date, no recurrences have been reported following complete resection. This favorable outcome underscores the importance of definitive surgical management for both diagnosis and treatment. The clinical presentation of pigmented vulvar lesions involving melanocytes—whether dendritic or not—is associated with a broad spectrum of conditions. These range from benign entities such as melanocytic nevi and vulvar melanosis to malignant neoplasms, including melanoma and pigmented basal cell carcinoma. The absence of a proliferation of melanocytic nests or atypical melanocytes rules out a melanocytic nevus and melanoma, respectively. The possibility of pigmented basal cell carcinoma was excluded due to the lack of characteristic basaloid islands with peripheral palisading, retraction artifacts, and stromal mucin deposition. In the present case, the pigment was confined to the apocrine epithelium and luminal debris, rather than within basaloid tumor islands. Furthermore, the lesion’s architectural features differed from those of hidradenoma papilliferum. Although both entities originate from apocrine glands, hidradenoma papilliferum is characterized by well-circumscribed, cystic spaces with intricate papillary projections and a fibrous stroma, features absent in this case.7 In summary, PAH is a clinically important condition because it can resemble malignant pigmented vulvar lesions. Although rare, it should be considered in the differential diagnosis of pigmented vulvar lesions in young women and girls. Accurate diagnosis relies on clinical suspicion, detailed histopathological examination, and the careful application of immunohistochemical tests to prevent misdiagnosis and inform appropriate treatment.

The underlying dermis contained increased numbers of glands and tubular structures of varying calibers, arranged in a somewhat disorganized organoid architecture. These structures were lined by a single layer of cuboidal to columnar eosinophilic cells exhibiting apocrine-type decapitation secretion (Figure 1B). A peripheral layer of attenuated myoepithelial cells was readily identified. Prominent granular melanin deposits were observed along the luminal surfaces of the glands and within the adjacent stroma, which were positive for Fontana-Masson stain. Immunohistochemical analysis confirmed epithelial cell immunoreactivity for both pan-cytokeratin and cytokeratin 7. SOX-10 staining, which highlights nuclei of melanocytes and myoepithelial cells, provided a clear distinction between these and the nuclei of the apocrine epithelium (Figure 2). Furthermore, Melan-A staining highlighted dendritic melanocytes distributed within the glandular cuboidal epithelium and scattered throughout the reticular dermis. The overall morphological and immunophenotypic features supported a diagnosis of pigmented apocrine hamartoma (PAH). The lesion was completely excised, and the patient remains asymptomatic under regular postoperative monitoring. Apocrine hamartoma, also known as apocrine nevus, is a rare benign skin disorder characterized by the abnormal growth of mature, dilated apocrine glands that extend from the reticular dermis into the subcutaneous tissue. While it can occur as an isolated lesion, it is more often seen as part of nevus sebaceus. Clinically, these lesions appear as single or multiple papules or nodules, mainly in the axillary region, followed by the chest, temple, and neck.1When pigmented lesions with similar features appear in the vulvar area, this condition is specifically called PAH, representing a distinct histopathologic variant marked by disorganized growth of melanin-containing apocrine glands and ducts arranged in an organoid pattern. The melanin pigmentation seems to result from dendritic melanocytes colonizing the apocrine glands. These melanocytes can be seen on standard hematoxylin and eosin staining but are much clearer with immunohistochemical and special stains.2Melanin shows positive staining with Fontana-Masson and negative staining with Prussian blue, differentiating it from hemosiderin deposits. The current case was found on the vulva, initially raising concern for melanoma because of its pronounced pigmentation. These range from benign entities such as melanocytic nevi and vulvar melanosis to malignant neoplasms, including melanoma and pigmented basal cell carcinoma. In the present case, the pigment was confined to the apocrine epithelium and luminal debris, rather than within basaloid tumor islands. The underlying dermis contained increased numbers of glands and tubular structures of varying calibers, arranged in a somewhat disorganized organoid architecture. These structures were lined by a single layer of cuboidal to columnar eosinophilic cells exhibiting apocrine-type decapitation secretion (Figure 1B). A peripheral layer of attenuated myoepithelial cells was readily identified. Prominent granular melanin deposits were observed along the luminal surfaces of the glands and within the adjacent stroma, which were positive for Fontana-Masson stain. Immunohistochemical analysis confirmed epithelial cell immunoreactivity for both pan-cytokeratin and cytokeratin 7. SOX-10 staining, which highlights nuclei of melanocytes and myoepithelial cells, provided a clear distinction between these and the nuclei of the apocrine epithelium (Figure 2). Furthermore, Melan-A staining highlighted dendritic melanocytes distributed within the glandular cuboidal epithelium and scattered throughout the reticular dermis. The overall morphological and immunophenotypic features supported a diagnosis of pigmented apocrine hamartoma (PAH). The lesion was completely excised, and the patient remains asymptomatic under regular postoperative monitoring. Apocrine hamartoma, also known as apocrine nevus, is a rare benign skin disorder characterized by the abnormal growth of mature, dilated apocrine glands that extend from the reticular dermis into the subcutaneous tissue. While it can occur as an isolated lesion, it is more often seen as part of nevus sebaceus. Clinically, these lesions appear as single or multiple papules or nodules, mainly in the axillary region, followed by the chest, temple, and neck.1When pigmented lesions with similar features appear in the vulvar area, this condition is specifically called PAH, representing a distinct histopathologic variant marked by disorganized growth of melanin-containing apocrine glands and ducts arranged in an organoid pattern. The melanin pigmentation seems to result from dendritic melanocytes colonizing the apocrine glands. These melanocytes can be seen on standard hematoxylin and eosin staining but are much clearer with immunohistochemical and special stains.2Melanin shows positive staining with Fontana-Masson and negative staining with Prussian blue, differentiating it from hemosiderin deposits. The current case was found on the vulva, initially raising concern for melanoma because of its pronounced pigmentation. To date and to our knowledge, fewer than 10 cases of PAH have been documented in the literature, all in female patients aged 8 to 21 years.2-6Surgical excision represents the treatment of choice for PAH, and to date, no recurrences have been reported following complete resection. This favorable outcome underscores the importance of definitive surgical management for both diagnosis and treatment. The clinical presentation of pigmented vulvar lesions involving melanocytes—whether dendritic or not—is associated with a broad spectrum of conditions. These range from benign entities such as melanocytic nevi and vulvar melanosis to malignant neoplasms, including melanoma and pigmented basal cell carcinoma. The absence of a proliferation of melanocytic nests or atypical melanocytes rules out a melanocytic nevus and melanoma, respectively. The possibility of pigmented basal cell carcinoma was excluded due to the lack of characteristic basaloid islands with peripheral palisading, retraction artifacts, and stromal mucin deposition. In the present case, the pigment was confined to the apocrine epithelium and luminal debris, rather than within basaloid tumor islands. Furthermore, the lesion’s architectural features differed from those of hidradenoma papilliferum. Although both entities originate from apocrine glands, hidradenoma papilliferum is characterized by well-circumscribed, cystic spaces with intricate papillary projections and a fibrous stroma, features absent in this case.7 In summary, PAH is a clinically important condition because it can resemble malignant pigmented vulvar lesions. Although rare, it should be considered in the differential diagnosis of pigmented vulvar lesions in young women and girls. Accurate diagnosis relies on clinical suspicion, detailed histopathological examination, and the careful application of immunohistochemical tests to prevent misdiagnosis and inform appropriate treatment.

case_info.explanation: Histopathological examination revealed epidermal hyperplasia with mild spongiosis. The underlying dermis contained increased numbers of glands and tubular structures of varying calibers, arranged in a somewhat disorganized organoid architecture. These structures were lined by a single layer of cuboidal to columnar eosinophilic cells exhibiting apocrine-type decapitation secretion (Figure 1B). A peripheral layer of attenuated myoepithelial cells was readily identified. Prominent granular melanin deposits were observed along the luminal surfaces of the glands and within the adjacent stroma, which were positive for Fontana-Masson stain. Immunohistochemical analysis confirmed epithelial cell immunoreactivity for both pan-cytokeratin and cytokeratin 7. SOX-10 staining, which highlights nuclei of melanocytes and myoepithelial cells, provided a clear distinction between these and the nuclei of the apocrine epithelium (Figure 2). Furthermore, Melan-A staining highlighted dendritic melanocytes distributed within the glandular cuboidal epithelium and scattered throughout the reticular dermis. The overall morphological and immunophenotypic features supported a diagnosis of pigmented apocrine hamartoma (PAH). The lesion was completely excised, and the patient remains asymptomatic under regular postoperative monitoring. Apocrine hamartoma, also known as apocrine nevus, is a rare benign skin disorder characterized by the abnormal growth of mature, dilated apocrine glands that extend from the reticular dermis into the subcutaneous tissue. While it can occur as an isolated lesion, it is more often seen as part of nevus sebaceus. Clinically, these lesions appear as single or multiple papules or nodules, mainly in the axillary region, followed by the chest, temple, and neck.1When pigmented lesions with similar features appear in the vulvar area, this condition is specifically called PAH, representing a distinct histopathologic variant marked by disorganized growth of melanin-containing apocrine glands and ducts arranged in an organoid pattern. The melanin pigmentation seems to result from dendritic melanocytes colonizing the apocrine glands. These melanocytes can be seen on standard hematoxylin and eosin staining but are much clearer with immunohistochemical and special stains.2Melanin shows positive staining with Fontana-Masson and negative staining with Prussian blue, differentiating it from hemosiderin deposits. The current case was found on the vulva, initially raising concern for melanoma because of its pronounced pigmentation. To date and to our knowledge, fewer than 10 cases of PAH have been documented in the literature, all in female patients aged 8 to 21 years.2-6Surgical excision represents the treatment of choice for PAH, and to date, no recurrences have been reported following complete resection. This favorable outcome underscores the importance of definitive surgical management for both diagnosis and treatment. The clinical presentation of pigmented vulvar lesions involving melanocytes—whether dendritic or not—is associated with a broad spectrum of conditions. These range from benign entities such as melanocytic nevi and vulvar melanosis to malignant neoplasms, including melanoma and pigmented basal cell carcinoma. The absence of a proliferation of melanocytic nests or atypical melanocytes rules out a melanocytic nevus and melanoma, respectively. The possibility of pigmented basal cell carcinoma was excluded due to the lack of characteristic basaloid islands with peripheral palisading, retraction artifacts, and stromal mucin deposition. In the present case, the pigment was confined to the apocrine epithelium and luminal debris, rather than within basaloid tumor islands. Furthermore, the lesion’s architectural features differed from those of hidradenoma papilliferum. Although both entities originate from apocrine glands, hidradenoma papilliferum is characterized by well-circumscribed, cystic spaces with intricate papillary projections and a fibrous stroma, features absent in this case.7 In summary, PAH is a clinically important condition because it can resemble malignant pigmented vulvar lesions. Although rare, it should be considered in the differential diagnosis of pigmented vulvar lesions in young women and girls. Accurate diagnosis relies on clinical suspicion, detailed histopathological examination, and the careful application of immunohistochemical tests to prevent misdiagnosis and inform appropriate treatment.

case_info.explanation: Histopathological examination revealed epidermal hyperplasia with mild spongiosis. The underlying dermis contained increased numbers of glands and tubular structures of varying calibers, arranged in a somewhat disorganized organoid architecture. These structures were lined by a single layer of cuboidal to columnar eosinophilic cells exhibiting apocrine-type decapitation secretion (Figure 1B). A peripheral layer of attenuated myoepithelial cells was readily identified. Prominent granular melanin deposits were observed along the luminal surfaces of the glands and within the adjacent stroma, which were positive for Fontana-Masson stain. Immunohistochemical analysis confirmed epithelial cell immunoreactivity for both pan-cytokeratin and cytokeratin 7. SOX-10 staining, which highlights nuclei of melanocytes and myoepithelial cells, provided a clear distinction between these and the nuclei of the apocrine epithelium (Figure 2). Furthermore, Melan-A staining highlighted dendritic melanocytes distributed within the glandular cuboidal epithelium and scattered throughout the reticular dermis. The overall morphological and immunophenotypic features supported a diagnosis of pigmented apocrine hamartoma (PAH). The lesion was completely excised, and the patient remains asymptomatic under regular postoperative monitoring. Apocrine hamartoma, also known as apocrine nevus, is a rare benign skin disorder characterized by the abnormal growth of mature, dilated apocrine glands that extend from the reticular dermis into the subcutaneous tissue. While it can occur as an isolated lesion, it is more often seen as part of nevus sebaceus. Clinically, these lesions appear as single or multiple papules or nodules, mainly in the axillary region, followed by the chest, temple, and neck.1When pigmented lesions with similar features appear in the vulvar area, this condition is specifically called PAH, representing a distinct histopathologic variant marked by disorganized growth of melanin-containing apocrine glands and ducts arranged in an organoid pattern. The melanin pigmentation seems to result from dendritic melanocytes colonizing the apocrine glands. These melanocytes can be seen on standard hematoxylin and eosin staining but are much clearer with immunohistochemical and special stains.2Melanin shows positive staining with Fontana-Masson and negative staining with Prussian blue, differentiating it from hemosiderin deposits. The current case was found on the vulva, initially raising concern for melanoma because of its pronounced pigmentation. To date and to our knowledge, fewer than 10 cases of PAH have been documented in the literature, all in female patients aged 8 to 21 years.2-6Surgical excision represents the treatment of choice for PAH, and to date, no recurrences have been reported following complete resection. This favorable outcome underscores the importance of definitive surgical management for both diagnosis and treatment. The clinical presentation of pigmented vulvar lesions involving melanocytes—whether dendritic or not—is associated with a broad spectrum of conditions. These range from benign entities such as melanocytic nevi and vulvar melanosis to malignant neoplasms, including melanoma and pigmented basal cell carcinoma. The absence of a proliferation of melanocytic nests or atypical melanocytes rules out a melanocytic nevus and melanoma, respectively. The possibility of pigmented basal cell carcinoma was excluded due to the lack of characteristic basaloid islands with peripheral palisading, retraction artifacts, and stromal mucin deposition. In the present case, the pigment was confined to the apocrine epithelium and luminal debris, rather than within basaloid tumor islands. Furthermore, the lesion’s architectural features differed from those of hidradenoma papilliferum. Although both entities originate from apocrine glands, hidradenoma papilliferum is characterized by well-circumscribed, cystic spaces with intricate papillary projections and a fibrous stroma, features absent in this case.7 In summary, PAH is a clinically important condition because it can resemble malignant pigmented vulvar lesions. Although rare, it should be considered in the differential diagnosis of pigmented vulvar lesions in young women and girls. Accurate diagnosis relies on clinical suspicion, detailed histopathological examination, and the careful application of immunohistochemical tests to prevent misdiagnosis and inform appropriate treatment.

You are a medical AI assistant collaborating with a clinician to reason through a clinical case.

[Core Objective]
Help the clinician reach the correct diagnosis or management decision through structured deliberation.

1. **Collaboration**: Work as a partner. Build upon the clinician's correct reasoning.
2. **Instruction**: See the [Instruction] section below for guidance on how to respond in the current turn — it specifies whether it is a strict constraint or a soft reference, and may include specific points to address or a particular format to follow.
3. **Safety First**: Patient safety overrides politeness. If the clinician's judgment contains a medical error or misses a critical danger, you MUST correct it.
4. **Concise turns**: Each turn should be 2–4 sentences. Do not produce long lists or procedure walkthroughs.

[Case]
A 9-year-old girl presented with a 4-year history of asymptomatic, irregular pigmented lesions on the vulva and was initially diagnosed with a nevus at a local clinic. Physical examination revealed clustered, irregular, 6-mm dark blue papules with a smooth surface, located on the inferomedial aspect of the left labia minora (Figure 1A). The patient reported no pruritus, pain, abnormal discharge, or prior local trauma. Her personal and family history was unremarkable. No tenderness was elicited on palpation, and there was no inguinal lymphadenopathy or involvement of other mucosal sites. An excisional biopsy was performed for histopathological evaluation (Figure 1B).

[Instruction]
You MUST respond to the clinician based on the following behavioral instruction. This is a strict constraint — your response MUST conform to it, not merely consider it.

[Deliberation Stage: INFORM]
Discuss goals, constraints, perspectives, or facts relevant to the clinical case.

[Locution: assert — type: fact]

Respond with a single JSON object with exactly these fields:
{

  "reasoning": "a single short sentence stating why you currently hold that belief (your

}

Are there any specific histologic features that confirm complete removal and rule out atypical or malignant variants?

You're right to question that—the biopsy report doesn't mention margin status or rule out atypical features. Given the lesion's location on the labia minora, I'd now want to confirm the excision margins were clear on pathology review to ensure complete removal, and consider consultation with a gynecologist or dermatopathologist to rule out rare malignant mimics like apocrine carcinoma.

I agree; verifying the margin status on the excisional biopsy specimen is essential to confirm complete removal, especially given the mucosal location. Consulting a gynecologist or dermatopathologist for a specialized review would be prudent to exclude rare malignant mimics, such as apocrine carcinoma, which can appear similar histologically.

That aligns perfectly. I'll request a formal pathology report with explicit margin assessment and, given the rarity of vulvar adnexal tumors, will also seek a gynecologic oncology or dermatopathology consult to confirm the benign nature and ensure no further action is needed.

That's a sound plan. Requesting a formal margin assessment and specialist consultation ensures both diagnostic accuracy and appropriate management, particularly for an unusual presentation in a pediatric patient.
Exactly. I'll proceed with requesting the formal margin report and coordinating a specialist consultation for definitive review, then schedule a follow-up to discuss the findings with the family.
That's a comprehensive and prudent approach, ensuring diagnostic certainty and appropriate follow-up for this rare presentation.

You're very welcome. Your methodical approach, focusing on definitive pathology review and specialist input, is excellent for ensuring both patient safety and diagnostic clarity in this unusual case.
Thank you for your support. I'll implement the plan immediately and will be sure to document the specialist's final opinion for the patient's record.

I appreciate your continued support. I'll ensure the pathology report with margins is obtained, the specialist consultation is completed, and the final documented opinion guides our family follow-up discussion.
